topic: Google tests Gemini 4 Carbon AI secretly
headline_marked: [[Google secretly tests Gemini 4 Carbon]], its next AI chatbot, on public users
headline: Google secretly tests Gemini 4 Carbon, its next AI chatbot, on public users
summary: The unreleased Gemini 4 Carbon, codenamed "Argon 4", has been active on Arena, a platform where users blindly compare and vote on AI chatbot responses, allowing Google to gauge public preference before launch.
details: Google has been secretly testing its upcoming AI chatbot, Gemini 4 Carbon, on Arena, a public platform for blind AI comparisons. The model, identified by TestingCatalog under the alias "Argon 4", has been active since Saturday, allowing Google to gather user feedback before an official launch.

Arena facilitates blind pairwise comparisons where users submit a prompt and choose the better of two anonymous AI outputs. This method captures user preference, speed, and perceived usefulness, offering insights that traditional static benchmarks often miss.

TestingCatalog observed that "Argon 4" appeared to be one of the strongest systems among recent contenders on the platform. This public head-to-head trial approach has become increasingly important for AI labs like Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic.

Google has a history of staged rollouts, sometimes revealing model names or codenames before formal releases. The interval between such a public discovery and an official launch can vary from hours to days or longer.

Public preference tests on platforms like Arena provide real-world insights into how users rank an AI assistant when branding is removed. This feedback is crucial for Google, which integrates Gemini across consumer chat, workspace tools, and developer APIs.

If Gemini 4 Carbon performs well in these blind tests, Google can market it as a proven advancement. Conversely, if it underperforms, engineers have time to refine its behavior before a formal release, ensuring a stronger product.

topic: NYT sues Brave over AI content scraping
headline_marked: [[The New York Times sues Brave]] over alleged scraping and AI content sales
headline: The New York Times sues Brave over alleged scraping and AI content sales
summary: The lawsuit alleges Brave scraped subscriber-only and public content, then monetized it by selling access to AI companies for training and grounding, and enabled paywall circumvention.
details: The New York Times has filed a lawsuit against Brave Software, alleging unauthorized scraping and reproduction of its journalism. The complaint, dated November 2, 2026, claims Brave distributed this material, including content behind a paywall.

The Times further alleges that Brave monetized this collected publisher material by offering it through its Search API to AI companies and other customers. This was for purposes like AI model training and "grounding" — supplying source material for AI-generated answers.

A key allegation is that Brave enabled paywall circumvention, allowing users to access Times content by bypassing its access controls. The lawsuit contends Brave continued this conduct despite receiving cease-and-desist notices.

This case highlights the evolving landscape of content use by AI search. While traditional search engines crawl for indexing, AI search uses retrieved material to generate direct answers, potentially reducing direct visits to original publishers.

The lawsuit's focus on alleged collection, distribution, and sale of journalism for AI uses, especially paywalled content, could set a precedent. It challenges how far a search provider can extend its use of crawled content when serving AI customers.

For AI companies and search platforms, the case emphasizes the difference between accessing information for a link and using it as input for answer generation. Publishers are increasingly seeking control over training, retrieval, citations, and licensing.
